summary: Explains how the Network Information Center at SRI handled documents for the ARPANET community. It says all information the center holds is open to any network participant, and it suggests ways sites can help the flow of documents. It is administrative guidance from 1971 rather than a technical protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A library explains its rules: anyone can borrow books, here is how we sort them, and here is how you can help us keep the shelves tidy.

questions: what did the network information center do
how were early arpanet documents distributed
how were early arpanet documents cataloged
subtitle: How the Network Information Center numbered, cataloged and revised documents for the early ARPANET community.

tldr.problem: Network participants produced many reports, memos and manuals, and needed a shared way to find, cite and update them.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Information Center (NIC) assigns each item a unique NIC number, records it in a coded catalog, builds indexes, and sets conventions for revising documents.
tldr.outcome: The RFC asks participants to supply standard data such as author, date, abstract and keywords, and to revise documents by full pages rather than errata lists.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: R. Watson and J. North, SRI (ARC)

today: RFC 115 is an early administrative note from 1971, and its status is listed as Unknown. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes NIC practices of that time, not a current protocol.

sections.title: Open Information and the NIC Number
sections.content:
The NIC at the Stanford Research Institute (ARC) aims to ease the flow of information between Network sites. All information it handles is available to any Network participant, and anything it generates is unclassified. Anything sent to it is presumed unclassified and free of distribution limits, even if the document says otherwise.

Each item gets a serial NIC number. It has no intrinsic meaning, not even necessarily an indication of sequence of issue. It is a unique identifier for referring to the item, indexing it and filing it numerically.
sections.plainLanguage: Every paper gets its own number, like a library card number for a book. The number is just a name tag, not a ranking.

sections.title: The Catalog and Its Indexes
sections.content:
Each item is described with standard data elements (author, title, addressee, date, other numbers, keywords and abstract), coded and entered as an online system (NLS) statement. The files of these statements at ARC form the Master Catalog. The NIC Catalog is the subset coded *z2 NIC.

Programs at ARC sort and format the statements into the Current Catalog of the NIC Collection: a listing by author, a listing by NIC number, an author index and a keyword (titleworld) index. The indexes lead to the entire catalog, while listings can mark which items the Stations hold.

Groups of documents, such as the NWG/RFCs, are cataloged as subcollections that can be retrieved as a subset.
sections.plainLanguage: The library keeps a card for each paper with the writer, the title and a short summary. Then it sorts the cards in several ways so you can look things up.

sections.title: What Authors Should Supply
sections.content:
For memos, originators should supply the authors and their addresses, the addressees and their addresses, the date and the subject. A preassigned NIC number is desirable and can be obtained by calling NIC.

For reports and formal documents the essentials are the authors, addresses, title, date, abstract and keywords. The RFC asks for a short abstract of 150 to 200 words. Keywords should preferably come from a standard thesaurus, and when a document supersedes an earlier one, the author should say so.
sections.plainLanguage: When you hand in a paper, write your name, the date and a short summary on it. That way the librarian does not have to guess.

sections.title: Functional Documents and Revisions
sections.content:
A functional document keeps a constant title and function while its contents change, for example the NIC Catalog and the Directory of Network Participants. Authors of documents expected to change are urged to use a looseleaf format.

For a substantial revision, a new document is published with a new NIC number and a notation such as supercedes NIC 5621. For a few changed pages, each new or revised page carries the original number and a revision date. Inserted pages are numbered to fit (such as 5.1, 5.2) and deleted pages are replaced by a single page noting the deletion.

Revisions are made only by whole pages or more. NIC will not revise its own publications with errata lists and strongly recommends against their use by others.
sections.plainLanguage: If a book changes a little, you swap the pages and write the date on them. If it changes a lot, you make a new book with a new number.
